meta.note: Policy options. Dollar amounts are MODELED estimates sized to be realistic for a city of Hollister's size, except where confidence is 'verified'. Meter effects are game-design values, not forecasts.

community.name: The Fiscal Hawk
community.line: I want this fixed, not postponed.
community.likedLine: This one actually closes the gap. I'm satisfied.
community.dislikedLine: This postpones the problem more than it fixes it.

community.name: The Public Safety Advocate
community.line: Response times are not a line item to me.
community.likedLine: You protected the people who answer the calls.
community.dislikedLine: Public safety comes out of this worse than it went in.

community.name: The Neighborhood Voice
community.line: A city people leave isn't saving money.
community.likedLine: The neighborhoods can live with this.
community.dislikedLine: The neighborhoods are the ones paying for this.

community.name: The Business Voice
community.line: Don't balance this on the people who build here.
community.likedLine: You found savings before you found my wallet.
community.dislikedLine: Every answer here was a new tax or a new fee.

community.name: The Labor Ally
community.likedLine: Nobody lost a livelihood over this.
community.dislikedLine: This still comes out of the people who do the work.

actions.name: Voluntary separation incentives
actions.desc: Pay retirement and resignation incentives instead of ordering layoffs.
actions.consequence: Institutional knowledge walks out the door. You backfill the critical posts later at a premium.
actions.realNote: This is the approach Hollister actually took for FY 2026-27.

actions.name: Freeze all vacant positions
actions.desc: Hold every unfilled position citywide, including sworn vacancies.
actions.consequence: Cheapest real money on the board. It also quietly shrinks the city by attrition.
actions.realNote: Hollister eliminated 31 budgeted vacant positions in FY 2025-26 for about $6M.

actions.name: Lay off 12 non-safety positions
actions.desc: Reduction in force across administration, parks and public works.
actions.consequence: Fast, certain savings. It costs you the room and most of your workforce goodwill.

actions.name: Four-day City Hall week
actions.desc: Close City Hall on Fridays and move staff to a 36-hour schedule.
actions.consequence: Utilities and overtime drop. Residents find the counter closed when they need it.

actions.name: Overtime and scheduling reform
actions.desc: Rebuild shift schedules to cut callback and mandatory overtime.
actions.consequence: Real savings without a layoff, but it needs union agreement and a year to land.

actions.name: Contract out park maintenance
actions.desc: Move turf, landscape and restroom maintenance to a private contractor.
actions.consequence: Cheaper per acre. Response to problems gets slower and less accountable.

actions.name: Defer street maintenance one year
actions.desc: Skip this year's slurry seal and overlay program.
actions.consequence: Pavement that fails costs roughly four times as much to rebuild as to maintain. This is a loan from your own streets.

actions.name: Defer fleet and equipment replacement
actions.desc: Keep patrol cars, engines and street sweepers one more year.
actions.consequence: Maintenance costs climb and an engine out of service is a response time problem.

actions.name: Suspend non-essential travel and training
actions.desc: Cancel conferences and discretionary professional development.
actions.consequence: Small money. Certifications lapse and recruitment gets harder.

actions.name: Cut library and community center hours
actions.desc: Drop to four open days a week and end evening hours.
actions.consequence: Highly visible. It is the cut residents notice first and remember longest.

actions.name: Freeze administrative hiring
actions.desc: No backfills in finance, HR, IT or the clerk's office.
actions.consequence: It also slows the overdue audit catch-up, and lenders are watching that.

actions.name: Move to a regional fire services JPA
actions.desc: Shift fire operations into a joint powers authority with neighboring agencies.
actions.consequence: Shares overhead across agencies. You also give up direct control of your own fire service.

actions.name: Energy retrofit and solar agreement
actions.desc: LED conversion and a solar power purchase agreement on city facilities.
actions.consequence: Low risk, no service loss. It takes about a year to show up in the numbers.

actions.name: Restructure outstanding debt
actions.desc: Refinance and re-amortize existing obligations to lower annual payments.
actions.consequence: Lower payments now, more interest paid in total. A fiscal emergency does not get you good terms.

actions.name: Cut the City Manager's office budget
actions.desc: Reduce executive staffing, car allowances and discretionary accounts.
actions.consequence: Small money, large signal. Residents read this one as good faith.

actions.name: Full cost-recovery fee study
actions.desc: Reset building, planning and engineering fees to the true cost of service.
actions.consequence: Building permits alone bring in $3.7M. Resetting fees to the true cost of service is defensible and council-approvable, and the development community will fight it.

actions.name: Modernize the business license tax
actions.desc: Update a flat-rate schedule that has not changed in decades.
actions.consequence: The business license tax raises $240,000 on a flat-rate schedule that has not changed in decades. Moving to gross receipts could half again that. Small businesses feel it as a rate increase.

actions.name: First responder fee for medical calls
actions.desc: Bill insurers when fire units respond to medical emergencies.
actions.consequence: Common practice statewide. Residents still experience it as a bill for calling 911.

actions.name: Step up code enforcement and citations
actions.desc: Fund an additional code officer and enforce existing citation authority.
actions.consequence: Revenue from enforcement reads as a shakedown whether or not it is one.

actions.name: Lease rooftop and cell tower rights
actions.desc: Lease space on city water tanks and rooftops to carriers.
actions.consequence: Free money, small money. There is no reason not to do this.

actions.name: Raise the hotel tax to 12%
actions.desc: Increase transient occupancy tax from 10% to 12%.
actions.consequence: The hotel tax raises $975,000 today, so two points adds about $195K. Visitors pay it, not residents — the easiest ballot measure on this board.

actions.name: Cannabis business tax
actions.desc: Tax gross receipts of licensed cannabis businesses.
actions.consequence: Depends entirely on how many operators actually open here.

actions.name: Utility users tax at 3%
actions.desc: A 3% tax on electric, gas and telecom bills.
actions.consequence: The largest ongoing revenue available to you. Residents pay it on every bill, every month.

actions.name: Add a half-cent sales tax
actions.desc: A half-cent add-on to the local transactions and use tax.
actions.consequence: Measure W's one cent brings in $9.68M, so a half cent is worth roughly $4.8M. Hollister is already at 9.25%, and this is a hard ask in a fiscal emergency.

actions.name: Sell surplus city property
actions.desc: Dispose of city-owned parcels no longer used for operations.
actions.consequence: You can only sell it once, and you will never buy it back at this price.

actions.name: Borrow $11M from impact fee funds
actions.desc: An interfund loan from restricted impact fee funds to the General Fund.
actions.consequence: This is cash, not a fix. It is repayable by June 30, 2027 at 4%, and the capital projects those fees were collected for wait.
actions.realNote: On October 2, 2026 the Hollister City Council declared a fiscal emergency and approved exactly this: $18M from impact fee funds, $11M of it to the General Fund.

actions.name: Spend down the contingency
actions.desc: Release the $1.2M contingency held in the Non-Departmental budget.
actions.consequence: It is right there in the adopted budget and it is the easiest million you will ever find. It is also the only thing standing between you and the next unbudgeted pump station failure.
actions.realNote: The FY 2026-27 Approved Budget carries a $1,200,000 contingency line.

actions.name: Cancel city event funding
actions.desc: Zero out the $500,000 events budget.
actions.consequence: Hollister without its events calendar saves real money and costs the downtown businesses that depend on those weekends.
actions.realNote: The FY 2026-27 Approved Budget carries a $500,000 event expenditures line.
